cases.title: RUNE
cases.lede: An open source platform for building automations. I built the execution core: the small language that reads a node graph, the schema that stores it, and the Go workers that run it all at once.
cases.friction: Automating anything still assumes you know distributed systems. The tools that hide that, like Zapier and n8n, put it behind a subscription that gets expensive fast.
cases.fix: A visual canvas backed by a small language, run by workers that execute nodes concurrently, with each node's state visible while it runs.
cases.result: Free and self hostable, so the bill doesn't climb at exactly the moment the automation starts being useful.

cases.title: Gmail customer data bot
cases.lede: A firm had someone reading every inbound email and retyping customer details into a database by hand.
cases.friction: Four hours of somebody's day, every day, and the data still arrived late and inconsistent. The real cost was the salary plus every mistake that followed downstream.
cases.fix: An agent reads each message, works out what kind it is, pulls the fields that matter, checks them, and writes straight into the database.
cases.result: Four hours a day became a few minutes of looking over the exceptions. Nobody retypes anything now.
cases.note: Client work, so the code and the screenshots stay private.

cases.title: ASU ROAR
cases.lede: System architect on a competition Mars rover. Same instinct, pointed at hardware: find the broken link in the chain, then fix the chain.
cases.friction: Localisation and mapping were dead because the ROS transform tree was malformed, and the command link kept dropping in the middle of a run.
cases.fix: Rebuilt the transform tree, wrote a UART to CAN interfacer for the Jetson, then designed and RF tested a mesh network for the link.
cases.result: Mapping came back, the link held through the run, and over a hundred recruits went through two workshops I wrote.

patterns.heading: What I'm hired to do.
patterns.intro: Most of the hundred plus projects are undocumented or under NDA, but the shapes repeat. These four cover nearly all of them.

items.title: Instant reporting
items.before: Staff assembling the same PDF report by hand, every single week.
items.after: Now it generates on demand and mails itself out, and the hours that used to go into it go somewhere useful.

items.title: Data pipelines
items.before: Copy and paste between an API, a spreadsheet, and a calculation nobody quite trusts.
items.after: Collected through an API or a scraper, cleaned up, run through the real calculation, and published as the output people actually asked for.

items.title: Spreadsheet to app
items.before: A fragile workbook that only one person in the company can safely open.
items.after: Same logic, but behind a real interface the whole team can use without breaking anything.

items.title: Process audit
items.before: “We know it's slow, we just don't know where.”
items.after: I map how the work really flows, then tell you honestly which parts are worth automating and which ones aren't.

steps.title: Audit
steps.body: Sit with the process as it really runs. Time it. Find where the hours are going.

steps.title: Map
steps.body: Draw the flow people actually follow, not the one on the org chart. They usually differ.

steps.title: Automate
steps.body: Scripts, APIs, agents, workers. Whatever the job needs, and nothing it doesn't.

steps.title: Hand over
steps.body: Documented, owned by them, still running long after I've moved on.

about.heading: A computer engineer who kept taking freelance work.
body: I graduated in computer engineering from Ain Shams this year, and I freelanced the whole way through. That taught me something a degree doesn't: how to build for people who don't care how it works, only that their afternoon is free again.

I like hard, niche problems, and I pick things up quickly. Apps Script, then Python, then agents, then Go workers and a rover's transform tree. I'm a recovering perfectionist, so shipping on time is the thing I actively practise. And I do my best work on a good team.
